title: The contract management framework
objectives: Define PPP contract management, when it applies, and why it is critical to VfM.
Name the four components of the contract management framework.
Explain how and when the contract management team should be set up, and the characteristics and skills it needs.
Distinguish the roles of the private partner, the government, the Contract Manager and the Contract Administrator, including what the government must not do.
Describe the Contract Management Manual, information systems (MIS), relationship and stakeholder management, and grievance mechanisms.

sections.heading: 1. What PPP contract management is and why it matters
sections.body:
**PPP contract management** is the procuring authority overseeing the Project Company's delivery of the services defined in the **output specifications**, while ensuring ongoing **affordability**, **Value for Money (VfM)** and proper management of **risk transfer**, and managing the effects of changes in the external environment. It has two dimensions: carrying out the contract, and **proactive management** that anticipates future needs and reacts well to unforeseen events. In the Guide, contract management applies **from contract signature until the end of the contract**.

It also includes activities outside the contract text, especially **stakeholder** work: addressing stakeholders' needs and expectations, keeping communications active and inclusive, and building their buy-in. For the private partner, good practice means balancing competing constraints: **scope, quality, schedule, budget, resources and risks**. If one changes, at least one other is usually affected. For example, a shorter schedule often needs a bigger budget, or else reduced scope or quality.

**Why it matters.** Contract management is often the **“forgotten child”** of PPP programs: attention goes to preparation and procurement, with celebrations at financial close. But the service is actually built and delivered during implementation. Failure to manage the contract **will erode VfM** and may undermine the project's objectives.

The **risk allocation** is at the heart of the relationship and must be managed over the whole life of the project, to:
- enforce, clarify or modify it when unforeseen risks arise;
- make sure the private partner bears and mitigates its risks;
- monitor and manage the risks the government keeps.

Good monitoring shows the private partner that the government is an **informed and vigilant counterparty**, and it lets savings be found and shared (where the contract allows). It matters to the private partner too, because many private partners become **complacent** over time. Contract management also feeds lessons into future PPPs, and it includes monitoring **evolving climate risks**, for example through the maintenance history.

sections.heading: 2. The four components of the framework
sections.body:
The Guide divides contract management into **four main components**:

| Component | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Establishing governance and the contract management team** | Sets up the team, its structure, roles and responsibilities, resources, skills, training and continuity. |
| **Contract administration** | Monitors, reports and ensures that contract obligations are met; manages underperformance, risks, payment of the unitary charge, variations, disputes, benchmarking and market testing; uses a contract administration manual and checklists. |
| **Relationship management** | Keeps continuous engagement between the public and private partners through communication protocols, partnership behaviours and practical problem solving, so that trust and respect last over the project's life. |
| **Performance management** | Assesses whether services meet the required standards, whether remedies work, and whether there are trends; links monthly monitoring to payment. |

All four sit under **continuous monitoring and performance**. The rest of this lesson follows the first three components; performance monitoring in construction and operations is covered in later lessons.

sections.heading: 3. Setting up the contract management team
sections.body:
Whatever the project's size or structure, the procuring authority **must establish a dedicated team** with the skills to manage long-term risks and maintain VfM. A common mistake is to assume the PPP contract is **self-regulating and self-reporting**, because it places most obligations on the private partner. This leads to weak contract management and lower benefits. In the Chapman's Peak toll road case, the government was responsible for an environmental approval and had to pay a minimum revenue guarantee while it was outstanding. The payments far exceeded what a specialist contract management unit would have cost.

**Three characteristics of the team:**
- **Mandate**: a clear mandate to act for the government, through internal delegation or even legislation.
- **Contractual standing**: the PPP contract itself empowers the team to act as the government's representative and exercise specific rights.
- **Resources**: enough human and financial resources to do this well.

The design depends on the **scale** of the project (for example asset value), its **administrative complexity** (cross-border or cross-agency), and the **extent of risk retained** by the government. These factors must be considered **before contract award and signing**, because the team should be involved in the stages that follow. A single-project team suits very large, complex or unique projects; one team for several projects suits smaller, less complex projects in the same or similar sectors.

**Skills needed** (a multidisciplinary team): technical, administrative, legal, financial (for example refinancing), communication and insurance skills, plus expertise on climate indicators and climate KPIs.

**Timing through the PPP cycle:**
- **Identification**: define contract management requirements and discuss the budget.
- **Appraisal**: describe the function at least preliminarily, outline staff needs and secure an indicative budget for the whole contract term.
- **Structuring**: **appoint the Contract Manager**, identify other members and produce a detailed **Contract Management Manual**.
- **Tender**: future team members take part in negotiations on operational requirements and outputs.
- **End of Tender**: the team is **fully in place**, the final manual (with method statements, monitoring arrangements and quality plans) is complete, communication channels and protocols with the private partner are agreed, and training is done. Note: the manual stays in **draft until commercial close** (contract signature), so that it matches the signed contract. It is finalised after signature and updated as the deal moves to financial close.

Early set-up matters because most of the **tender team leaves** after award or financial close. Early involvement transfers their knowledge, builds a stronger negotiating position, and avoids pitfalls such as not understanding the private partner's solution or a payment mechanism the team never helped design.

sections.heading: 4. Governance and who does what
sections.body:
**Governance.** Several public bodies support contract management: the **Ministry of Finance** oversees fiscal commitments and exposure; the **PPP Unit** gives oversight and guidance; **sector regulators** monitor compliance with sector standards. Good practice creates **layers of interaction** at different levels, so that strategic disagreements do not disrupt daily work. An example structure: a **steering committee** for strategic issues (quarterly to annual), a **management committee** for ordinary issues (monthly to quarterly) and an **operational management team** for day-to-day issues. The public team should be continuous, constructive and cooperative, but **vigilant against opportunistic behaviour**.

**The private partner** must report in the format the government requires, as set out in the contract. It should set up a **Quality Management System (QMS)**, with a **Management Information System (MIS)** as a large part of it.

**What the government must not do.** The government **must not get involved in the private partner's actual decision making and execution**, because this would undermine the **risk transfer**. It also should not prescribe how the private partner structures itself, because lenders and shareholders already impose governance discipline. But it **should be prescriptive** on: **changes in shareholding**; having suitably **qualified personnel**; changes in the **financial structure** (distributions, refinancing); and **reporting requirements**.

**The government's role**: monitor that obligations are met by the right party; monitor performance and apply the remedies for non-performance; define team roles; manage changes both permitted and not provided for in the contract; and provide for dispute resolution.

**Team roles:**
- **Primary roles** relate to the contract: represent the government and enforce its rights, monitor performance and apply payment and penalty mechanisms, maintain securities and insurances, manage disputes and changes, oversee assets, adjust user charges, and report on financial performance and **contingent fiscal obligations**.
- **Secondary roles** relate to wider public policy: coordinate across government, watch the policy and legislative environment, integrate the project with other public services, and communicate with end users and communities.
- The **Contract Manager** leads daily, with delegated authority and enough seniority; is **accountable for all decisions**; decides day-to-day matters within the delegation and **escalates** extraordinary decisions with cost or risk impacts; makes sure major decisions (such as dispute resolution or amending the contract) follow proper consultation and legal requirements; and develops the manual and annual oversight plans. The role is likely **full time**.
- On **larger and more complex projects**, the Contract Manager may be supported by a **Contract Administrator** and a **Knowledge and Training Specialist**. Other specialist skills can be brought in when needed.
- The **Contract Administrator** needs good organisation and an eye for detail. It handles files and documents, financial management, records of risks, the manual's procedures for claims, and meetings.
- The **Knowledge and Training Specialist** identifies initial and ongoing training. There are two types of training: a general introduction to PPPs and the project cycle, and specific training (contract and project management, payment mechanisms, risk analysis, change management, dispute resolution).

**Continuity.** PPPs often last 20 years or more, so the team that starts the project will rarely finish it. **Succession planning** and written policies, procedures and manuals keep the knowledge inside government. If the government does not appoint skilled, empowered staff, the result is **under-resourcing**, especially in the busy early stages, and poor contract management.

**Disclosure.** The team's roles include disclosing information of two types: information about the contract at closure (for example contract summaries and full contracts at financial close), and **ongoing performance information** until expiry or termination (for example independent engineer and auditor reports, performance and financial data). **Full contract disclosure should be the default**, with exceptions only for specifically exempt information. Any renegotiation should be disclosed transparently, showing changes in risk allocation, costs, tariffs and government exposure.

sections.heading: 5. The Contract Management Manual and information management
sections.body:
The **Contract Management Manual** is a collection of policies and procedures for managing the PPP contract. It is written in **plain language**, explains the authority's duties and how to monitor the private partner, and sets internal procedures between departments (for example between the operational team and the accounts department for payments).

Key rules:
- It must be **read together with the signed contract** and aligned with it. It **never replaces the contract**.
- It gives a **strategic context**, including a summary of “the deal” that explains the **intent** behind the contract, not just its clauses.
- It **highlights actions** on a rolling basis in an **obligations register**, **aligns resources** to the most critical risks, **supports governance** and reporting, and **collects contract management tools**.
- It is a **dynamic document**, reviewed and updated regularly.
- It is a **knowledge management** tool for succession and for transitions between stages. New team members should be trained in its use.

**Information.** Most information comes from the Project Company; the government's job is mainly to **receive it and verify that it is accurate and consistent**. The contract should be clear and prescriptive on the **detail, format and deadlines** of reports, avoiding **too much** information (costly to produce and analyse) and **too little** (the government cannot do its job). Where there are social commitments such as gender targets, reporting should require disaggregated data.

**Management Information System (MIS).** To make the MIS work, the government should: state in the tender documents that it expects transparent access for the whole contract; discuss bidders' planned MIS during procurement; ask the private partner to build suitable interfaces such as web portals; and **test-run the MIS before operations start**. The private partner should upgrade it regularly and avoid expensive bespoke systems. But if a consortium member already has a suitable low-cost system, insisting on a different one may not be VfM.

sections.heading: 6. Relationship, stakeholder and grievance management
sections.body:
PPPs last a long time and involve many parties. **Relationship risk** is hard to quantify: damage usually follows poor communication and a loss of trust. The principles apply in both construction and operations.

**Good relationships:**
- Start with a **collaborative, not adversarial**, attitude. If one party is adversarial, the other tends to copy it.
- Put in place procedures to **resolve issues quickly and informally** from the start. **Formal dispute procedures come only if consensus fails.**
- Communication is the main attribute. Misunderstandings are common, for example an authority blaming slow response times on cost cutting when the specified times were wrong.
- Record the **partnering principles** in the Contract Management Manual.

**Stakeholder management.** Project success depends on stakeholders' perceptions. The team should assess stakeholders' **influence and expectations** and engage them accordingly: senior politicians (the project needs a **political champion**), the general public, end users (including their willingness to pay in user-pays projects), **project-affected persons**, senior civil servants, and NGOs, unions and the press. Communities are **not homogeneous**: women, men, young, elderly and disabled people may need different approaches.

Even where the private partner carries a stakeholder risk, the team can **support** it. For example, if the Project Company needs a permit from another department, the team can help that department understand the project, **provided it gives no assurance that the permit will be granted**.

Involve end users early, since poor consultation can cause delays and risks such as objections to fees, land and permit problems, community opposition or staff opposition. Keep a **contacts database**, consider a project website, and use an experienced communications specialist.

**Grievance mechanisms** give community members, users and workers a **formal, transparent** way to raise concerns, ideally from the start of environmental and social assessment until the end of the project. To be inclusive, they should be free, simple, publicised, available through several channels, anonymous and safe to access.

example.title: Illustrative case: the Eastfield Schools PPP
example.body:
Imagine a province procuring ten schools as one PPP. The PPP unit suggests appointing a Contract Manager only after financial close, to save money. The province's advisers disagree. They recommend appointing her during structuring, so that she helps design the payment mechanism and writes the draft Contract Management Manual.

After signature, most of the tender team moves to other projects, but the Contract Manager already knows the deal. Early in construction, head teachers complain that the Project Company chose cheaper classroom furniture. Some officials want to instruct the company which supplier to use. The Contract Manager explains that this would interfere with the Project Company's execution and weaken risk transfer. Instead, she checks the output specification. The furniture meets it, so she records the teachers' concerns and discusses them at the monthly management committee.

Later, the Project Company plans to refinance its debt. Because the contract requires government approval of changes to the financial structure, the Contract Manager escalates the decision to the steering committee with the Ministry of Finance.

examTraps.trap: Thinking the PPP contract is self-regulating, so a small or late contract management team is enough.
examTraps.fix: The Guide calls this a common mistake that leads to weak contract management and lost VfM. A dedicated, skilled team must be in place by the end of the Tender phase.

examTraps.trap: Believing the government should control how the private partner does its work.
examTraps.fix: The government monitors outputs and obligations but must not get involved in the private partner's decision making or execution, as this weakens risk transfer. It is prescriptive only on shareholding, personnel, financial structure and reporting.

examTraps.trap: Treating the Contract Management Manual as a substitute for the contract.
examTraps.fix: The manual is read together with the contract, must be aligned with it, and never replaces it. It explains intent, actions, resources and procedures.

examTraps.trap: Confusing the Contract Manager with the Contract Administrator.
examTraps.fix: The Contract Manager leads, holds delegated authority, is accountable for decisions and escalates major ones. The Contract Administrator supports with files, records, finance administration and meetings.

examTraps.trap: Mixing up primary and secondary roles of the contract management team.
examTraps.fix: Primary roles concern the contract itself (enforce rights, monitor performance, manage changes and disputes). Secondary roles concern wider public policy and stakeholders to whom the private partner is not accountable.

keyTerms.meaning: The authority's oversight of the Project Company's delivery of the output specifications, protecting affordability, VfM and risk transfer, from signature to contract end.
The dedicated public team, with mandate, contractual standing and resources, that manages the PPP contract for the government.
The senior person with delegated authority who leads the team daily, is accountable for decisions and escalates extraordinary ones.
The team member who supports the Contract Manager with documents, records, financial administration and meetings.
A plain-language set of policies and procedures, aligned with but never replacing the contract, used to manage it and transfer knowledge.
A rolling list, kept in the manual, of the most immediate and critical actions the authority must take.
The IT system, usually run by the private partner, that records activities and gives reliable performance data to the government.
The hard-to-quantify risk that poor communication and lost trust damage the partnership and reduce VfM.
A formal, transparent process for communities, users and workers to raise concerns or complaints about the project.

summary: Contract management runs from signature to contract end and protects affordability, VfM and risk transfer.
It is often the forgotten child of PPP programs; neglect erodes VfM.
Four components: team and governance, contract administration, relationship management, performance management.
The team needs mandate, contractual standing and resources; the Contract Manager is appointed in structuring and the team is fully in place by the end of the tender.
The government must not interfere in the private partner's execution, but is prescriptive on shareholding, personnel, financial structure and reporting.
The Contract Management Manual is aligned with the contract, never replaces it, and is updated regularly.
Relationships should be collaborative, with informal issue resolution first and formal disputes only when consensus fails.

slides.title: What contract management is
points: Oversee delivery of the output specifications
Protect affordability, VfM and risk transfer
slides.narration: Welcome to contract management. The tender is over and the contract is signed. Now the real work begins. Contract management means the authority oversees how the Project Company delivers the services in the output specifications, while protecting affordability, value for money and the agreed risk transfer. It runs from signature until the end of the contract, often twenty years or more. It is not only reactive. Good contract managers also look ahead, anticipate future needs, and respond well when the unexpected happens.

slides.title: The forgotten child
points: Attention usually stops at financial close
Risk allocation must be managed for life
slides.narration: The Guide calls contract management the forgotten child of many PPP programs. Governments celebrate at financial close, but the service is actually built and delivered afterwards. If the contract is not managed, value for money erodes. The risk allocation needs attention for the whole project life: enforcing it, clarifying it when new risks appear, and watching the risks the government keeps. And good monitoring shows the private partner that the government is informed and vigilant, which keeps everyone performing.

slides.title: Four components
slides.narration: The framework has four main components. First, establishing the governance and the contract management team. Second, contract administration: making sure obligations are met, managing payments, variations, risks and disputes. Third, relationship management: keeping communication and trust alive between the public and private partners. And fourth, performance management: checking that services meet the required standards and that remedies actually work. Keep these four in mind; exam questions often ask which component an activity belongs to.

slides.title: Building the team early
points: Team fully in place by tender end
slides.narration: A common mistake is to think the contract will manage itself. It won't. The authority needs a dedicated team with a clear mandate, standing under the contract, and enough resources. Timing matters. The Contract Manager should be appointed during structuring, and the whole team should be in place by the end of the tender. Why so early? Because most of the tender team leaves after award or financial close. If the contract managers were there from the start, the knowledge stays in government.

slides.title: Hands off the execution
points: Prescriptive on shareholding, finance, personnel, reporting
slides.narration: Here is a key principle. The government monitors, but it must not get involved in the private partner's actual decisions and execution. If it starts telling the company how to do the work, it weakens the risk transfer, and the company may later blame the government. There are some exceptions where the government should be prescriptive: changes in shareholding, having qualified staff, changes in the financial structure such as refinancing, and the timing and content of reports.

slides.title: Who does what
slides.narration: Inside the team, the Contract Manager is the leader. They hold delegated authority, make day-to-day decisions, and escalate big decisions with cost or risk impacts to the right level of government. They are accountable for every decision. The Contract Administrator supports them with files, records and meetings. The team's primary roles are about the contract itself, like enforcing rights and managing changes. Its secondary roles are about wider public policy, like coordinating with other departments and talking to communities.

slides.title: The Contract Management Manual
points: Plain language, aligned with the contract
Never a substitute for the contract
slides.narration: The Contract Management Manual is the team's everyday guide. It's written in plain language, explains the intent behind the deal, lists the critical actions in an obligations register, and sets the procedures to follow. But remember: it is always read together with the contract, and it never replaces it. It must be updated regularly. And because staff will change over twenty years, the manual is also a knowledge tool. New team members should be trained to use it.

slides.title: Information and relationships
points: Clear reporting: not too much, not too little
slides.narration: Most information comes from the Project Company, so the government's job is to check it is accurate. The contract should set the detail, format and deadlines: not so much that it becomes costly, not so little that the government cannot do its job. Test the information system before operations begin. Finally, relationships. Start collaborative, not adversarial. Solve problems quickly and informally, and use formal dispute procedures only when agreement fails. And don't forget stakeholders and a fair grievance mechanism.

quiz.question: A finance ministry argues that, because the PPP contract puts most obligations on the private partner, the procuring authority only needs one part-time officer to manage it. What does the Guide say about this view?
options: It is correct, as the lenders will monitor the private partner
It is a common mistake that weakens management and cuts benefits
It is acceptable if the contract includes a strong penalty regime
It is correct for availability-based projects but not user-pays ones
quiz.explanation: The Guide says assuming the contract is self-regulating and self-reporting is a mistake that results in weak contract management and reduced benefits. A dedicated team with mandate, standing and resources is needed regardless of project size or structure.

quiz.question: Which activity belongs to the contract administration component of the contract management framework?
options: Defining job profiles and training needs for the team
Developing partnership protocols and behaviours
Identifying stakeholders' influence and expectations
Managing unitary charge payments and contract variations
quiz.explanation: Contract administration monitors that obligations are met and manages underperformance, risks, payment of the unitary charge and variations. Job profiles and training belong to establishing the team; partnership protocols belong to relationship management.

quiz.question: A procuring authority is structuring a hospital PPP. When should it appoint the future Contract Manager?
options: In the Structuring Phase, to help design the manual and payments
After financial close, once the private partner starts construction work
At service commencement, when the monitoring of performance begins
Only if serious problems arise during the first year of operations
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the Contract Manager should be appointed in the Structuring Phase and the team should be fully in place by the end of the Tender phase. Late appointment causes pitfalls such as poor understanding of the contract and payment mechanism.

quiz.question: Which set lists the three characteristics of a contract management team described in the Guide?
options: Independence, neutrality and technical expertise
Budget, schedule and quality
Mandate, contractual standing and resources
Monitoring, reporting and enforcement
quiz.explanation: Table 7.1 lists mandate (authority to act for government), contractual standing (empowered under the PPP contract) and resources (human and financial). The other sets mix unrelated concepts.

quiz.question: During construction, a procuring authority's engineers dislike the Project Company's choice of construction method and want to instruct it to use a different one. The chosen method is expected to meet the output specifications. What should the contract management team do?
options: Instruct the new method, since the government is paying for the asset
Approve the method formally so the government shares responsibility
Continue monitoring outputs and avoid directing the Project Company's execution
Suspend payments until the Project Company agrees to change
quiz.explanation: The government must not get involved in the private partner's decision making and execution, because this adversely affects the risk transfer. It should monitor against the output specifications instead.

quiz.question: A Project Company's shareholders plan to sell a majority stake to a new investor. How should the procuring authority's contract be designed to handle this?
options: With explicit obligations or approval requirements for changes in shareholding
With no rules, since the private partner's structure is its own business
With a ban on all share transfers for the whole contract term
With a requirement that the government buys any shares for sale
quiz.explanation: Although the government should generally not prescribe how the private partner structures itself, the Guide lists changes in shareholding as an area where it should be prescriptive, through explicit obligations or formal approvals. A total ban is not what the Guide recommends.

quiz.question: A new Contract Manager reads the Contract Management Manual and finds that one procedure conflicts with the signed PPP contract. What should happen?
options: Follow the manual, as it reflects the authority's internal policy
Ask the Project Company to amend the contract to match the manual
Apply whichever document was written most recently
Correct the manual so it is aligned with the contract
quiz.explanation: The manual must always be read together with the contract, be aligned with it and never substitute for it. It is a dynamic document that should be reviewed and updated regularly.

quiz.question: Which task is a secondary role of the contract management team rather than a primary role?
options: Enforcing the payment and penalty mechanism
Monitoring the policy and legislative environment of the project
Ensuring securities and insurances are properly maintained
Managing variations and amendments to the contract
quiz.explanation: Secondary roles relate to broader public policy, such as monitoring the policy and legislative environment and coordinating across government. Enforcing payments, maintaining securities and managing changes relate to the contract itself, so they are primary roles.

quiz.question: The Project Company must obtain a permit from the environment ministry, a risk it bears under the contract. How can the contract management team help appropriately?
options: Guarantee to the Project Company that the permit will be granted
Take over the permit application itself to speed things up
Take no action, since the risk sits with the Project Company
Brief the ministry on the project but give no promise on the permit
quiz.explanation: Even when the private partner bears a stakeholder risk, the team can play a supportive role by informing the other department about the project, provided it gives no assurance that the permit will be granted. Taking over or guaranteeing would shift the risk back to government.

quiz.question: The Contract Manager and the Project Company's manager disagree about slow response times. There is no clear breach yet. What should they do first?
options: Use the informal issue-resolution steps agreed at the outset
Start the formal dispute resolution procedure immediately
Refer the matter straight to the national courts
Apply the maximum penalty to encourage faster responses
quiz.explanation: The Guide says procedures for quickly and informally rectifying issues should be in place from the outset, and formal dispute management should come into play only if mutual consensus cannot be reached. Misunderstandings, such as wrongly specified response times, are common.

quiz.question: According to the Guide, what is the second dimension of PPP contract management, beyond carrying out the contract?
options: Renegotiating the contract every five years to reflect market prices
Replacing the private partner's management when performance falls
Proactive management of future needs and unforeseen situations
Reviewing the procurement decision to confirm the PPP route was right
quiz.explanation: The Guide says a second dimension of contract management is proactive management to anticipate future needs and to react appropriately to unforeseen situations. Routine renegotiation or replacing the private partner's managers are not part of this definition (Ch 7 §1).

quiz.question: For the purposes of the PPP Guide, over what period is PPP contract management applied?
options: From financial close until the service commencement date
From contract signature until the end of the PPP contract
From the Appraisal Phase until the end of construction
From service commencement until the handback of the asset
quiz.explanation: The Guide states that PPP contract management is applied from contract signature until the end of the PPP contract. It is not limited to construction or to operations (Ch 7 §1).

quiz.question: A road PPP must open two months earlier than planned because of a national event, but the authority has no extra budget. Based on the Guide's view of competing project constraints, what is most likely needed?
options: A reduction in scope or targeted quality to finish in less time
No change at all, since schedule and budget are independent
An increase in the length of the operations period
A transfer of the schedule risk back to the procuring authority
quiz.explanation: The Guide explains that if the schedule is shortened, the budget usually rises; if a budget increase is not possible, scope or quality may be reduced. Constraints are linked, so changing one usually affects at least one other (Ch 7 §1, Box 7.2).

quiz.question: Why does the Guide call contract management the "forgotten child" of many national PPP programs?
options: Most PPP contracts do not mention contract management at all
Contract management is usually handed to the lenders after signature
Attention goes to procurement and the celebration of financial close
It is only needed for the small number of PPPs that get into trouble
quiz.explanation: The Guide says great attention is paid to preparation and procurement, with celebrations after financial close, although services are built and delivered during implementation. Contract management is needed on every PPP, not only troubled ones (Ch 7 §2).

quiz.question: Five years into operations, an unforeseen risk arises that the contract does not clearly allocate. What does the Guide say about managing the risk allocation in this situation?
options: It is fixed at financial close and can never be revisited
The unforeseen risk automatically passes to the private partner
The unforeseen risk automatically passes to the lenders
It must be enforced, clarified or modified when unforeseen risks arise
quiz.explanation: The initial risk allocation must be managed over the whole life of the project, including enforcing, clarifying or modifying it when unforeseen risks or consequences arise. There is no automatic transfer to either party (Ch 7 §2).

quiz.question: A new technology could cut the running costs of a PPP hospital. The contract contains a savings-sharing clause. According to the Guide, what makes it possible for the government to get a share of these savings?
options: A unilateral cut in the unitary charge by the authority
Proper monitoring of the project by the government
A new tender for the hospital's operations
An instruction to the Project Company to adopt the technology
quiz.explanation: The Guide says savings can be achieved and shared only if there is proper monitoring by the government, provided the contract allows sharing. Unilateral payment cuts or instructions would breach the contract and weaken risk transfer (Ch 7 §2).

quiz.question: A PPP team wants to track whether climate change is affecting a coastal road. What does the Guide recommend monitoring during the Contract Management Phase?
options: Only the traffic counts reported by the toll system
Only the lenders' annual financial model updates
The maintenance history provided by the private partner
The bid prices of other coastal road projects
quiz.explanation: The Guide recommends monitoring the maintenance history from the private partner to identify changes in climate risk and to inform future projects on resilience benefits. All partners are responsible for monitoring evolving climate risks (Ch 7 §2).

quiz.question: An authority's team is agreeing communication routes with the Project Company and developing partnership protocols and behaviours. Which component of the contract management framework is this?
options: Relationship management
Contract administration
Performance management
Establishing governance and the team
quiz.explanation: Figure 7.1 places communication protocols, partnership protocols and behaviours, and practical problem resolution under relationship management. Contract administration covers payments, variations and disputes (Ch 7 §3).

quiz.question: A team checks each month whether services meet the required standards, whether remedial measures work and whether any trends appear, and links this to payment. Which component of the framework is this?
options: Relationship management
Establishing governance and the team
Benchmarking and market testing
Performance management
quiz.explanation: Performance management assesses whether services meet the standards, whether remedies are effective and whether trends are evident, including monthly monitoring and payment. Benchmarking and market testing is an activity under contract administration, not a component (Ch 7 §3).

quiz.question: A regional government plans five small school PPPs of similar design in the same sector. How should it organize contract management?
options: A separate large team for each school from Identification onwards
No government team, with monitoring left to the lenders
A single contract management team for several of the projects
One team for construction and a new team for each year of operations
quiz.explanation: The Guide says one team for multiple projects is often preferable when projects are smaller, less complex and in the same or similar sectors. A single-project team suits very large, complex or unique projects (Ch 7 §3.1).

quiz.question: A ministry has created a contract management unit by law, but the signed PPP contract does not name it or give it any rights. Which characteristic of a contract management team is missing?
options: A clear mandate
Adequate resources
Technical independence
Contractual standing
quiz.explanation: Contractual standing means the PPP contract itself empowers the team to act as the government's representative and exercise rights. The law gives it a mandate, but without contract rights it lacks standing (Ch 7 §3.1, Table 7.1).

quiz.question: A ministry is designing the contract management team for a new cross-border rail PPP. Which set of factors does the Guide say will shape the team's mandate, contractual standing and resources?
options: Bidder numbers, tariff levels and the lenders' credit rating
Project scale, administrative complexity and retained risk
Contract length, the construction method and the design life
Political support, media interest and the number of users
quiz.explanation: The Guide says these functions depend on the scale of the project (for example the value of the assets), its administrative complexity, such as cross-border or cross-agency jurisdiction, and the extent of risk retained by government. The other sets are not the factors the Guide lists (Ch 7 §3.1).

quiz.question: A PPP project is in the Appraisal Phase. According to the Guide, what should happen to the contract management function at this point?
options: Describe it preliminarily and secure an indicative budget
Appoint the full team and finalise the Contract Management Manual
Agree communication protocols with the preferred bidder
Take no action until the preferred bidder is selected
quiz.explanation: In Appraisal the function should be described at least on a preliminary basis, staff needs outlined, and an indicative budget secured for the contract duration. The full team and final manual belong to the end of the Tender Phase (Ch 7 §3.1).

quiz.question: By the end of the Tender Phase, which of the following should the Guide expect to be complete?
options: The completion certificate issued and service commencement approved
The full team in place and communication protocols agreed
The first annual performance audit carried out and published
The first refinancing of the Project Company's debt approved
quiz.explanation: At the end of the Tender Phase the team should be fully in place, the final manual complete, communication channels and protocols agreed and training provided. Completion certificates and refinancing come much later (Ch 7 §3.1).

quiz.question: Negotiations with the preferred bidder are still changing some obligations, and commercial close has not yet happened. What should the authority do with the Contract Management Manual?
options: Finalise it now and make the contract match the manual
Delay any work on it until service commencement
Ask the preferred bidder to write and approve it
Keep it in draft and finalise it after commercial close
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the manual stays in draft until commercial close so that it reflects the obligations in the final signed contract, and it is finalised after that, with updates as the deal moves to financial close (Ch 7 §3.1, note 9).

quiz.question: The contract management team of a metro PPP was not involved when the payment mechanism was designed during structuring. Which pitfall does the Guide link to this?
options: A higher interest rate on the senior debt
Loss of the Project Company's insurance cover
Poorly monitored and executed financial management
An automatic right for bidders to challenge the award
quiz.explanation: The Guide lists poorly monitored and executed financial management as a pitfall when the contract management function was not involved in designing the payment mechanism at structuring. The other options are not linked to this (Ch 7 §3.1).

quiz.question: In the governance of PPP contract management, which body typically oversees the project's fiscal commitments and the public sector's financial exposure?
options: The Ministry of Finance
The sector regulator
The independent certifier
The Project Company's board
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the Ministry of Finance often oversees fiscal commitments and exposure, the PPP Unit gives oversight and guidance, and sector regulators monitor compliance with sector standards (Ch 7 §3.1.1).

quiz.question: A strategic disagreement about future tariff policy between senior officials and the Project Company's directors is starting to affect daily site meetings. What governance arrangement does the Guide recommend to prevent this?
options: One single meeting forum for every issue
Suspending daily meetings until the dispute is settled
Communication interfaces at different hierarchical levels
Moving all decisions to the Ministry of Finance
quiz.explanation: The Guide advises creating communication interfaces at several levels to mitigate personal conflicts and stop strategic disagreements from affecting day-to-day operations. A single forum mixes the levels, which is the problem (Ch 7 §3.1.1).

quiz.question: In the example governance structure in the Guide, which body deals with strategic issues and meets quarterly to annually?
options: The management committee
The operational management team
The contract administration unit
The steering committee
quiz.explanation: Figure 7.3 shows a steering committee for strategic issues (quarterly to annual), a management committee for ordinary issues (monthly to quarterly) and an operational management team for day-to-day issues (Ch 7 §3.1.1).

quiz.question: After signing, an authority tells the Project Company it wants monthly reports in a new format that the contract never mentioned. Why does the Guide say reporting requirements should instead be set in the PPP contract?
options: So the private partner can design compliant reporting systems
So the lenders can approve every report before it is sent
So the independent certifier can write the reports
So that no reports are needed during construction
quiz.explanation: The Guide says reporting requirements must be communicated in the contract so the private partner can design and implement a compliant reporting process and information systems. Adding new formats later is harder and may be a change (Ch 7 §3.2.1).

quiz.question: A procuring authority wants to tell the Project Company how many directors it must have and how its board committees should work. Why does the Guide advise against this?
options: Board structure is set by the independent certifier under the contract
Lenders and shareholders already impose governance discipline
The PPP Unit must approve all board appointments
Corporate governance rules apply only after handback
quiz.explanation: The government should be careful not to prescribe how the private partner structures itself, because the project finance structure imposes discipline: lenders and shareholders ensure good corporate governance. It is prescriptive only on areas such as shareholding and financial structure (Ch 7 §3.2.1).

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the steps the government should follow from the outset of a project, according to the Guide?
options: Clearly define the roles of its contract management team
Manage changes not provided for in the PPP contract
Provide for dispute resolution
Direct the Project Company's construction methods
quiz.explanation: The steps are: define team roles, monitor delivery, manage changes permitted and not provided for in the contract, and provide for dispute resolution. Directing construction methods would interfere with execution and weaken risk transfer (Ch 7 §3.2.2).

quiz.question: A Treasury asks the contract management team for a report on how a new guarantee in the PPP changes the government's possible future liabilities. Is this one of the team's roles?
options: Yes, but only as a secondary role linked to public policy
Yes, reporting on contingent fiscal obligations is a primary role
No, only the Project Company reports on liabilities
No, this is solely the independent certifier's role
quiz.explanation: Reporting on the contingent fiscal obligations accruing to the government, and any changes to them, is listed as a primary role because it relates to the contract itself (Ch 7 §3.2.2.1).

quiz.question: A Contract Manager faces a proposed change that would add significant cost and shift a major risk to the government. The decision is outside the manager's delegated authority. What should the manager do?
options: Escalate it to the appropriate level of government
Approve it quickly to keep the relationship positive
Reject it without consultation to protect the budget
Ask the Contract Administrator to decide instead
quiz.explanation: A good Contract Manager acts within delegated authority day to day, and elevates extraordinary decisions with cost or risk implications to the right level of government. The Administrator supports on administration and does not take such decisions (Ch 7 §3.2.2.2).

quiz.question: Which task does the Guide give to the Contract Manager rather than to the Contract Administrator?
options: Organizing files and managing documents
Keeping records of risks and their possible impacts
Preparing annual oversight plans, including audits
Organizing meetings and communications
quiz.explanation: The Contract Manager develops the manual, leads the team and prepares annual plans for specific oversight, including audits and reports on key risk areas. Files, risk records and meetings are Contract Administrator tasks (Ch 7 §3.2.2.2–3.2.2.3).

quiz.question: A newly recruited team member has no PPP experience. Who should identify her initial and ongoing training needs, and what two types of training does the Guide describe?
options: The Contract Administrator; legal training and engineering training
The Project Company; induction and health and safety training
The PPP Unit; procurement training and bid evaluation training
The Knowledge and Training Specialist; general and specific training
quiz.explanation: The Knowledge and Training Specialist identifies initial and ongoing training needs. The two types are an overall introduction to PPPs and the project lifecycle, and specific training on contract and project management, payment mechanisms, risk analysis and similar topics (Ch 7 §3.2.2.4).

quiz.question: A PPP runs for 25 years, and the Contract Manager will retire in three years. Which two elements does the Guide say support continuity of knowledge within government?
options: Longer employment contracts and higher salaries for the team
Handing all records to the Project Company for safekeeping
Succession planning and written policies, procedures and manuals
Re-tendering the contract management function every five years
quiz.explanation: Because the team that starts a long PPP will rarely finish it, the Guide names succession planning and putting policies, procedures and manuals in place as the two elements supporting continuity (Ch 7 §3.2.2).

quiz.question: A government wants to keep a new PPP contract confidential, although no part of it is specifically exempt. What does the Guide say about contract disclosure?
options: Contracts should be disclosed only at handback
Full contract disclosure should be the default
Only a one-page summary should ever be disclosed
Disclosure is optional and depends on the lenders
quiz.explanation: The Guide says full contract disclosure should be the default, with exceptions only for specifically exempt information. Renegotiations should also be disclosed transparently (Ch 7 §3.2.2.1).

quiz.question: What should the "summary of the deal" in a Contract Management Manual do, according to the Guide?
options: Explain the intent behind the contract's clauses
Replace the legal text of the contract for daily use
List only the penalty amounts for each type of failure
Record the bid prices of all the losing bidders
quiz.explanation: Box 7.3 says the manual should include a summary of the deal that illustrates the intent behind the contract and its key provisions, rather than simply repeating clauses. It never replaces the contract (Ch 7 §3.3.1).

quiz.question: Where should a Contract Manager record the most immediate and critical actions the authority must take, including items such as gateway reviews that go beyond the contract?
options: In the manual's obligations register
In the Project Company's quality management system
In the lenders' financial model
In the independent certifier's completion report
quiz.explanation: The manual must highlight, on a rolling basis, the most immediate and critical actions in an obligations register. These actions extend beyond the contract, for example gateway reviews during service delivery and before expiry (Ch 7 §3.3.1).

quiz.question: An authority is drafting reporting obligations and proposes that the Project Company send hundreds of daily data fields that nobody will analyse. What is the problem, according to the Guide?
options: Daily reporting is prohibited in PPP contracts
The data would breach the lenders' confidentiality rights
Too much information transfers design risk to the authority
Too much information is costly to produce and to analyse
quiz.explanation: The Guide warns against requiring too much information, which is costly for the private partner to produce and for the government to analyse, and too little, which limits the government's ability to do its job (Ch 7 §3.3.2).

quiz.question: A PPP contract includes gender targets for local hiring. What should its monitoring and reporting obligations require?
options: An annual statement that the targets are respected, without data
Reporting only if a complaint about hiring is received
Disaggregated data and regular progress reports on the targets
Reports on gender to the lenders instead of the authority
quiz.explanation: Where a contract includes social commitments such as gender specifications, reporting obligations should mandate disaggregated data collection and regular reports on progress, challenges and measures (Ch 7 §3.3.2).

quiz.question: A Project Company's new MIS will be the government's main window on performance. When should the authority test-run it?
options: After the first year of operations, once data exists
Before operations commence, to make sure it works
Only if the first performance report is late
At handback, to check the records are complete
quiz.explanation: The Guide says governments should test-run the private partner's MIS in advance of operations commencement to ensure it is functional. They should also stress transparent access in the tender documents (Ch 7 §3.3.3).

quiz.question: A consortium member already owns a proprietary MIS that can serve the project at low cost. The authority prefers a different system. What does the Guide suggest?
options: The authority must always insist on its own system
Proprietary systems are banned in PPP projects
The Project Company must build an expensive bespoke system
Insisting on a different system may not be VfM
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the private partner should generally avoid expensive bespoke MIS, but where a consortium member has an existing low-cost system, it may not be VfM for the government to insist on a different one (Ch 7 §3.3.3).

quiz.question: Consider these statements about relationship risk in PPPs. 1: It is easy to quantify because it appears in the risk matrix. 2: Damage to a relationship usually follows and worsens a reduction in mutual trust.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: The Guide says relationship risk cannot easily be quantified and is more complex than many other risks, so statement 1 is false. Damage usually follows and exacerbates a reduction in mutual trust, so statement 2 is true (Ch 7 §3.4).

quiz.question: From the first meeting, an authority's new team treats the Project Company as an opponent. What does the Guide warn is the likely result?
options: The other party copies the approach, harming both sides
The Project Company will perform better because of the pressure
The lenders will step in and replace the Project Company
The risk allocation will automatically move to the authority
quiz.explanation: Relationship management should start with a collaborative, not adversarial, attitude. If either party starts adversarially, the other may copy it, compromising the long-term interests of both (Ch 7 §3.4.1).

quiz.question: A new transport PPP program faces scepticism in parliament. Which stakeholder action does the Guide recommend for senior politicians?
options: Exclude politicians from all project communications
Ensure there is a political champion for the program or project
Treat politicians as low-interest, low-influence stakeholders
Ask the Project Company to lobby parliament directly
quiz.explanation: The Guide, citing EPEC, says the contracting authority should ensure there is a political champion. Senior politicians who can influence implementation are usually in the high interest/high influence category (Ch 7 §3.4.2).

quiz.question: A rural road PPP will affect elderly residents, young people and women traders differently. What does the Guide recommend for communication?
options: One standard message for the whole community
Communication only with the village leaders
Specific communication strategies for each relevant group
No consultation, since the private partner holds the risk
quiz.explanation: The Guide stresses that communities are not homogeneous; women, men, the young, the elderly and people with disabilities may have different interests, so specific strategies may be needed for each group (Ch 7 §3.4.2).

quiz.question: In a school PPP where the government is not the end user, why should the authority involve teachers and parents early?
options: Poor consultation can cause delays, objections and other risks
Early consultation moves the demand risk to the Project Company
Teachers must approve the final design under the Guide
Consultation replaces the need for a grievance mechanism
quiz.explanation: Inadequate consultation can delay implementation and limit the ability to mitigate risks such as public objection to fees, permit problems, community opposition and operational staff (for example teachers) objecting (Ch 7 §3.4.3).

quiz.question: A PPP team is designing a grievance mechanism. Which design choice does the Guide support to ensure equal access?
options: A small fee to discourage minor or repeated complaints
No fee, several ways to submit a complaint, and anonymity
A single online form, available in the official language only
Access limited to registered users of the service
quiz.explanation: Box 7.4 recommends not charging a fee, offering more than one submission method, ensuring anonymity, and enabling access for people who speak only the local language or cannot read (Ch 7 §3.4.4).
